bibl.title: Irrelevant Stimuli and Action Control: Analyzing the Influence of Ignored Stimuli via the Distractor-Response Binding Paradigm

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The distractor-response binding paradigm itself - a prime-probe protocol for separating distractor-based response retrieval from distractor inhibition.
span.quote: The paradigm of distractor-response binding was developed to specifically investigate the influence distractors that compete with a target stimulus for the response, have on action control.

span.label: How can distractor-based response retrieval and distractor inhibition be measured separately when studying how ignored stimuli influence human action control?
span.quote: In particular, this technique allows to disentangle the two mechanisms that have been discussed in the context of distractor processing, namely distractor inhibition and distractor based retrieval of responses.

span.label: method
span.quote: The distractor-response binding paradigm can be used to investigate this influence.

span.label: distractor-response binding
span.quote: The paradigm of distractor-response binding is useful to investigate influences of distractors that compete with the target stimulus for a response execution.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: The present article gives a detailed description of the paradigm used to analyze the distractor-based retrieval and distractor inhibition.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Re-encountering a stimulus that was bound into an event file retrieves the whole stored episode, including the response executed with it, so an ignored distractor can drive the current response.
span.quote: Re-encountering the stimulus of such an event file leads to a retrieval of the entire episode from memory, including the associated response 4-8 .

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Retrieval runs in parallel with the algorithm computing the required response, so the longer the response takes, the more often retrieval finishes in time to influence it - which is why slower tasks show larger binding effects.
span.quote: With longer lags between triggering response retrieval and execution of the response, the retrieval process is more likely to be completed before response execution 22 .

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Inhibiting the same distractor twice in a row carries after-effects that facilitate the second inhibition, producing a benefit that is independent of whether the response repeats.
span.quote: That is, an inhibition account 1,25 would predict, that inhibiting the same stimulus two times in a row should always lead to benefits because after effects from distractor inhibition on the prime should facilitate distractor inhibition on the probe.

span.label: A stimulus and a response executed close together in time are stored as one episodic trace, so re-encountering the stimulus retrieves the whole episode including the response
span.quote: Re-encountering the stimulus of such an event file leads to a retrieval of the entire episode from memory, including the associated response 4-8 .

span.label: Because the distractor is bound into the same trace as the target and response, the distractor alone can trigger retrieval of the target's response
span.quote: On the next encounter, any of these stimuli ( i.e. also the distractor stimulus) can trigger the retrieval of the entire event file including the target response.

span.label: Retrieval therefore helps when the response repeats and hurts when it changes, which is why the signature is an interaction rather than a main effect
span.quote: In contrast, if a change of response is required, repeating the distractor hampers responding as the distractor retrieves an incompatible response.

span.label: Inhibition predicts a benefit from distractor repetition that does not depend on response repetition, which is what makes the two mechanisms separable in one design
span.quote: This benefit effect of repeated distractors is, however, according to the inhibition theory independent of response repetition.

span.label: Retrieval runs in parallel with computing the required response, so slower tasks give retrieval more time to finish and produce larger effects
span.quote: This can be understood as a consequence of the retrieval process working in parallel to the algorithm that calculates the currently required reaction.

span.label: The factors that modulate the distractor-response binding effect are not yet fully specified.
span.quote: Yet, more research is necessary to define further modulating factors of the effect.

span.label: The paradigm has been validated in only one clinical sample (unpublished), so the trial numbers needed for individual-difference work are unknown.
span.quote: Therefore, it cannot be ruled out that higher numbers of trials are required for the investigation of inter-individual differences in the effect of distractor-response binding.

span.label: The effect fails if the gap between prime response and probe onset is too long
span.quote: No effect of distractor-response binding was found with an onset asynchrony of 1,500 msec 30 .

span.label: Grouping of target and distractor appears to be required, and the full set of modulating conditions is not yet known
span.quote: Yet, more research is necessary to define further modulating factors of the effect.

span.label: Only one clinical sample has been looked at, and that data is unpublished, so trial numbers for individual-difference work are unknown
span.quote: Therefore, it cannot be ruled out that higher numbers of trials are required for the investigation of inter-individual differences in the effect of distractor-response binding.

span.label: Error rates usually yield nothing, so the paradigm effectively rests on response times alone
span.quote: Yet, oftentimes, participants make very few errors and no significant effects are found in the error rates.

span.label: Trials repeating the target identity must be dropped from analysis to keep target-based bindings out, yet kept in the procedure to stop participants responding strategically
span.quote: Yet, to prevent strategic responding by participants, it can be useful to include trials with target repetition in the procedure.

span.label: The paradigm is modality-independent: the same binding effect and the same response-time modulation appear in visual, auditory and tactile versions, which the paper reads as evidence that the mechanism is central rather than perceptual
span.quote: Although mean response times modulate the effect, this modulation seems to be the same in previous visual, tactile, and auditory experiments (see Figure 4 ). These results also suggest that the effect evidences a rather central mechanism of action control.

span.label: distractor repetition effect - as an INTERACTION with response relation: the signature of retrieval, i.e. of distractor-response binding
span.quote: Thus, distractor-based retrieval is indicated by the interaction effect of response repetition × distractor repetition.

span.label: distractor repetition effect - as a MAIN EFFECT: the signature of inhibition, read off the same design and the same data
span.quote: While retrieval effects are evidenced by an interaction of response repetition and distractor repetition, distractor inhibition is measured as the main effect of distractor repetition.

span.label: response repetition - with the same target identity (RRi): excluded from analysis because target repetition would confound it
span.quote: Omit response repetition trials with target identity repetition ( i.e. RRi trials) to exclude influences of target identity repetition effects.

span.label: response repetition - with a different target from the same response category (RR): the condition actually analysed
span.quote: For trial type RR-DR, implement response repetition by presenting a target stimulus from the same response category on the prime and the probe display.

span.label: negative priming - under the inhibition account: residual inhibition of the former distractor makes responding to it harder
span.quote: Residual inhibition of the former distractor stimulus results in a disadvantage if a response to this inhibited stimulus is required on the probe 1,11 .

span.label: negative priming - under the retrieval account: a do-not-respond tag encoded with the distractor is retrieved and conflicts with responding
span.quote: For example, Neill assumed that the prime distractor is encoded together with a do-not-respond tag at the prime, which is then retrieved and in turn conflicts with responding to this stimulus if it is repeated as the probe target 14 .

span.label: builds-on → the negative priming paradigm (review by Fox)
span.quote: The distractor-response binding paradigm originates from research using the negative priming paradigm (for a review see Fox 10 ).

span.label: extends → the negative priming paradigm
span.quote: One advantage over the negative priming paradigm is that the paradigm of distractor-response binding can differentiate between effects of distractor inhibition and response retrieval 24 .

span.label: extends → the negative priming paradigm, from which this paradigm originates
span.quote: The distractor-response binding paradigm originates from research using the negative priming paradigm (for a review see Fox 10 ).

span.label: extends → the Stimulus Response Retrieval theory and the Theory of Event Coding
span.quote: More recently, the Stimulus Response Retrieval theory (SRR 15 ) assumed that distractors are integrated with and can trigger the retrieval of responses.

span.label: critiques → the pure inhibition account of negative priming, which cannot be separated from retrieval in that paradigm
span.quote: One difficulty with this paradigm has been that at least two different mechanisms can account for the negative priming effect.

span.label: instance —same-as→ event file
span.quote: The compound of stimulus and response is then stored as an “instance” 4 or “event file” 5,6 in episodic memory.

span.label: event file —part-of→ episodic memory
span.quote: Based on the Theory of Event Coding 16 , SRR proposes that target, distractor, and response features are encoded in one temporary episodic memory trace or event file .

span.label: distractor inhibition —part-of→ cognitive control
span.quote: Distractor inhibition is one of the core concepts of cognitive control 3 .

span.label: distractor-response binding —distinct-from→ negative priming
span.quote: The distractor-response binding paradigm originates from research using the negative priming paradigm (for a review see Fox 10 ).

span.label: distractor-response binding —contrasted-with→ negative priming
span.quote: One advantage over the negative priming paradigm is that the paradigm of distractor-response binding can differentiate between effects of distractor inhibition and response retrieval 24 .

span.label: Stimulus Response Retrieval theory —distinct-from→ Theory of Event Coding
span.quote: Based on the Theory of Event Coding 16 , SRR proposes that target, distractor, and response features are encoded in one temporary episodic memory trace or event file .

span.label: distractor inhibition —contrasted-with→ response retrieval
span.quote: In particular, this technique allows to disentangle the two mechanisms that have been discussed in the context of distractor processing, namely distractor inhibition and distractor based retrieval of responses.

span.label: distractor-response binding —operationalised-as→ response relation
span.quote: Thus, distractor-based retrieval is indicated by the interaction effect of response repetition × distractor repetition.

span.label: distractor inhibition —operationalised-as→ distractor relation
span.quote: While retrieval effects are evidenced by an interaction of response repetition and distractor repetition, distractor inhibition is measured as the main effect of distractor repetition.

span.label: response retrieval —operationalised-as→ event file
span.quote: On the next encounter, any of these stimuli ( i.e. also the distractor stimulus) can trigger the retrieval of the entire event file including the target response.

span.label: onset asynchrony —causes→ distractor-response binding
span.quote: On the other hand, it is crucial that the time between prime response and probe stimulus onset is sufficiently short.

span.label: selection task —causes→ distractor-response binding
span.quote: The effect is evidenced in sequential selection tasks by the influence distractor repetition has on performance depending on response repetition.

span.label: selective attention —causes→ distractor inhibition
span.quote: Once a stimulus is identified as being irrelevant, inhibition dampens the activation of the distractor representation 1 or blocks its access to the response system to reduce interference 2 .

span.label: do-not-respond tag —causes→ negative priming
span.quote: For example, Neill assumed that the prime distractor is encoded together with a do-not-respond tag at the prime, which is then retrieved and in turn conflicts with responding to this stimulus if it is repeated as the probe target 14 .

span.label: Gestalt principles —causes→ distractor-response binding
span.quote: Another prerequisite seems to be the presentation of target and distractor in a grouped fashion 19,21 .

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Enter probe response times into a 2 (Response Relation: repetition vs. change) × 2 (Distractor Relation: repetition vs. change) ANOVA.

span.label: interaction effect
span.quote: Thus, distractor-based retrieval is indicated by the interaction effect of response repetition × distractor repetition.

span.label: main effect
span.quote: A significant main effect of distractor repetition indicates an additional distractor inhibition effect.

span.label: standard error
span.quote: Error bars depict the standard error of the means.

span.label: outlier removal
span.quote: For the analyses of probe response times, only consider trials with correct responses to the prime and the probe and exclude anticipatory (below 200 msec) and outlier response times ( e.g. Tukey 26 ).

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The confidence interval is indicated by broken lines.

span.label: explained variance
span.quote: The continuous line indicates the function explaining 50% of the variance between the effects in the different experiments.

span.label: mean
span.quote: Distractor repetition effects are calculated as the mean response time in distractor change trials minus the mean response time in distractor repetition trials.

span.label: Repeating a distractor speeds responding when the same response must be repeated, because the distractor retrieves a compatible response.
span.quote: If the same response has to be given on the prime and probe, distractor repetition leads to better performance as compared to distractor change because the distractor retrieves a compatible response.

span.label: Repeating a distractor slows responding when the response must change, because the distractor retrieves the now-incompatible response.
span.quote: In contrast, if a change of response is required, repeating the distractor hampers responding as the distractor retrieves an incompatible response.

span.label: The paradigm's central advantage is that response retrieval shows up as the response-by-distractor interaction while distractor inhibition shows up as the distractor main effect, so the two mechanisms can be read off separately from the same design.
span.quote: While retrieval effects are evidenced by an interaction of response repetition and distractor repetition, distractor inhibition is measured as the main effect of distractor repetition.

span.label: Across 33 published experiments the binding effect grew larger as tasks got harder and mean response times got longer.
span.quote: The effects become larger with more difficult tasks and thus with longer response times.

span.label: A single function describes how response time modulates the binding effect in visual, auditory and tactile experiments alike, implying a central rather than modality-specific mechanism.
span.quote: Note that this modulation can be represented by the same function for all modalities.

span.label: The interval between the prime response and probe onset must be short: no binding effect appeared at an onset asynchrony of 1,500 msec.
span.quote: No effect of distractor-response binding was found with an onset asynchrony of 1,500 msec 30 .

span.label: Presenting target and distractor grouped together appears to be a precondition for the effect.
span.quote: Another prerequisite seems to be the presentation of target and distractor in a grouped fashion 19,21 .

span.label: Error rates usually carry no significant effects because participants commit too few errors.
span.quote: Yet, oftentimes, participants make very few errors and no significant effects are found in the error rates.

span.label: Shortening stimulus presentation to 300 msec, imposing an 800 msec response window, or varying the prime-probe gap between 150 and 350 msec all leave the result pattern intact.
span.quote: A response window of 800 msec does also not alter the result pattern 29 , and a variable period of 150 to 350 msec between prime response and probe onset has been used successfully, as well 28 .

span.label: Unpublished data from participants with autism spectrum disorder suggest the effect is obtainable in a clinical sample with the same number of trials.
span.quote: Unpublished data of participants with autism spectrum disorder give a first indication that the effect of distractor-response binding can be found with similar trial numbers in a clinical sample.

span.label: distractor-response binding
span.quote: These retrieval effects due to distractor repetition have been termed distractor-response binding .

span.label: negative priming effect
span.quote: In a negative priming paradigm, prime distractors that are repeated as targets on the probe lead to slower response times or more errors as compared to probe responses to targets that did not appear on the prime ( i.e. the negative priming effect).

span.label: event file
span.quote: Based on the Theory of Event Coding 16 , SRR proposes that target, distractor, and response features are encoded in one temporary episodic memory trace or event file .

span.label: instance
span.quote: The compound of stimulus and response is then stored as an “instance” 4 or “event file” 5,6 in episodic memory.

span.label: selective attention
span.quote: One important mechanism is selective attention, that is, the ability to discriminate between relevant and irrelevant information.

span.label: Stimulus Response Retrieval theory (SRR)
span.quote: More recently, the Stimulus Response Retrieval theory (SRR 15 ) assumed that distractors are integrated with and can trigger the retrieval of responses.

span.label: distractor inhibition (operationalised)
span.quote: While retrieval effects are evidenced by an interaction of response repetition and distractor repetition, distractor inhibition is measured as the main effect of distractor repetition.

span.label: event file
span.quote: SRR proposes that target, distractor, and response features are encoded in one temporary episodic memory trace or event file .

span.label: distractor repetition effect
span.quote: Distractor repetition effects are calculated as the mean response time in distractor change trials minus the mean response time in distractor repetition trials.

span.label: response relation (repetition vs. change between prime and probe)
span.term: response relation (repetition vs. change between prime and probe)
span.quote: Importantly, the factors response relation in the arrays of each pair (repetition vs. change) and distractor relation (repetition vs. change) are varied orthogonally.

span.label: distractor relation (distractor repetition vs. distractor change)
span.term: distractor relation (distractor repetition vs. distractor change)
span.quote: Prepare six different kinds of trial types ( i.e. prime probe sequences), orthogonally varying response relation (response repetition with same target vs. response repetition with different targets vs. response change) and distractor relation (distractor repetition vs. distractor change).

span.label: probe response time
span.quote: Enter probe response times into a 2 (Response Relation: repetition vs. change) × 2 (Distractor Relation: repetition vs. change) ANOVA.

span.label: probe error rate
span.quote: The same ANOVA can be used to analyze probe error rates.

span.label: stimulus arrangement
span.quote: Use the same stimulus arrangement for all displays throughout the experiment.

span.label: modulating factor (e.g. attention, distractor-target onset asynchrony, alerting signal) held constant on the probe
span.term: modulating factor (e.g. attention, distractor-target onset asynchrony, alerting signal) held constant on the probe
span.quote: If the effect a certain factor ( e.g. attention, distractor target onset asynchrony, an additional alerting signal, etc.) has on response integration with the distractor is of interest, this factor can be varied on the prime, while it is held constant on the probe.

span.label: target identity repetition (removed from analysis)
span.quote: Omit response repetition trials with target identity repetition ( i.e. RRi trials) to exclude influences of target identity repetition effects.

span.label: 180 trials — Total number of experimental trials produced by repeating each of the six trial types 30 times
span.quote: Do the assignments for each trial type and repeat this 30x, resulting in 180 trials.

span.label: 60 trials — Size of the practice block drawn at random before the main experiment
span.quote: Use a random sample of 60 trials for a practice block.

span.label: 33 experiments (27 visual, five auditory, one tactile) — Number and modality breakdown of the published experiments whose binding effects are summarised against mean response time
span.quote: Distractor-response binding effects in msec that were found in 33 experiments (27 using visual, five using auditory, and one using tactile stimuli) as a function of mean response times in the experiments.

span.label: 50% — Share of the between-experiment variance in binding effects explained by the fitted function of mean response time
span.quote: The continuous line indicates the function explaining 50% of the variance between the effects in the different experiments.

span.label: 1,500 msec — Prime-probe onset asynchrony at which no distractor-response binding effect was obtained
span.quote: No effect of distractor-response binding was found with an onset asynchrony of 1,500 msec 30 .

span.label: 300 msec — Fixed stimulus presentation duration that still reproduced the binding pattern
span.quote: Several experiments revealed the same pattern with stimulus presentation of 300 msec 19,32 .
